monopsony_power.label: Monopsony power in labour markets (single/dominant buyer of labour able to set wages below competitive level)

stages.name: Minimum wage and monopsony
stages.title: Minimum wage and monopsony
stages.sub: Why a minimum wage can raise both pay and jobs when one firm dominates hiring.

steps.q: A single dominant employer in a small town can set the wage it pays, rather than accept a market rate. To keep its wage bill low, does it pay workers the full value of what an extra worker adds, or less than that?
steps.wrong: The full value of what they add
steps.hint: Think about why a firm with wage-setting power would want to hold wages down.
steps.pre: So that dominant firm pays a wage that sits

steps.q: Because this firm holds wages down below the value each extra worker adds, does it hire as many workers as a competitive market would, or fewer?
steps.hint: Paying less than a worker is worth still limits how many the firm is willing to take on at that low wage.

steps.q: Looking at the usual minimum wage diagram, if the floor is set only slightly above this firm's own low wage, does it sit above or below the wage the firm was already choosing to pay?
steps.right: Above the wage it was paying
steps.wrong: Below the wage it was paying
steps.hint: The firm was choosing a wage lower than competitive; a floor just above that low wage is still higher than what it paid.

steps.q: This firm was hiring fewer workers than it should because wages were held too low. If a floor now forces it to pay closer to what workers add, what happens to jobs, compared to a normal minimum wage story?
steps.hint: Here the firm was under-hiring because wages were too low, not because wages were already competitive.
